title: Modulation of anomalous Hall angle in a magnetic topological semimetal
authors: Jinying Yang, Yanxing Shang, Xingchen Liu, Yibo Wang, Xuebin Dong, Qingqi Zeng, Meng Lv, Shen Zhang, Yang Liu, Binbin Wang, Hongxiang Wei, Yizheng Wu, Stuart Parkin, Gangqin Liu, Claudia Felser, Enke Liu, Baogen Shen
abstract: The anomalous Hall angle (θA) is a measure of the efficiency of converting a longitudinal driving current to a transverse spin-polarized Hall current. For anomalous Hall sensing, a large anomalous Hall angle can improve the sensitivity of magnetic field detection. However, modulation of this angle is challenging and magnetic materials typically have low angles of 0.1 to 3°. Here, we report modulation of the anomalous Hall angle in the magnetic Weyl semimetal Co3Sn2S2. We propose that the angle parameter tanθA can be formulated as a function of the product of electrical resistivity and anomalous Hall conductivity. Our scheme was utilized to demonstrate the modulation of tanθA up to a magnitude of 0.46, corresponding to an angle of around 25°. Microfabricated anomalous Hall devices using Fe-doped Co3Sn2S2 single-crystalline nanoflakes exhibit a high Hall sensitivity of 7028 μΩucm/T and a magnetic field detectability of 23.5 nT/Hz0.5 at 1 Hz.
summary: This work reports on modulating the anomalous Hall angle ($	heta_A$) in magnetic Weyl semimetals using $	ext{Co}_3	ext{Sn}_2	ext{S}_2$. By theoretically linking $	an	heta_A$ to the product of resistivity and anomalous Hall conductivity, the authors experimentally achieved a large angle (~25°) through controlled doping and thickness reduction. This results in highly sensitive magnetic field detectors for spintronic applications.
main_problem: The primary goal is to enhance the sensitivity of anomalous Hall sensors by maximizing the anomalous Hall angle ($	heta_A$), which quantifies current conversion efficiency.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated modulation of $	an	heta_A$ up to a magnitude of 0.46 (an angle of ~25°) in magnetic Weyl semimetals, leading to high magnetic field detectability ($23.5 	ext{ nT}/	ext{Hz}^{0.5}$).
method: The study combines theoretical modeling relating $	an	heta_A$ to the product of resistivity and anomalous Hall conductivity ($ho_{xx}\sigma^H_A$) with experimental measurements on fabricated nanoflakes.
model_or_system: The research focuses on magnetic Weyl semimetals, specifically $	ext{Co}_3	ext{Sn}_2	ext{S}_2$, which are synthesized into single-crystalline nanoflakes. Modulation is achieved by tuning both the intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity ($\sigma^H_A$) and the longitudinal resistivity ($ho_{xx}$) via doping or thickness reduction.
key_observables: Anomalous Hall angle ($	an	heta_A$), Hall sensitivity ($7028 \mu\Omega\cdot	ext{cm/T}$), and magnetic field detectability ($23.5 	ext{ nT}/	ext{Hz}^{0.5}$).
important_parameters: The maximum achievable $	an	heta_A$ is the key parameter, which depends on tuning both $ho_{xx}$ and $\sigma^H_A$.
main_assumptions: The anomalous Hall angle relationship is modeled as being proportional to the product of electrical resistivity and anomalous Hall conductivity ($	an	heta_A \propto ho_{xx}\sigma^H_A$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $	an	heta_A$ dependence on $ho_{xx}$ and $\sigma^H_A$, showing optimal modulation paths, while other figures detail temperature and thickness dependencies of the AHE signal.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem (enhancing $	heta_A$), develops a theoretical framework linking $	an	heta_A$ to material parameters ($ho_{xx}, \sigma^H_A$), presents experimental results showing modulation via doping/thickness, and concludes with high-sensitivity device metrics.
why_interesting: While the core physics is condensed matter transport (magnetotransport), the ability to engineer a macroscopic parameter like $	heta_A$ through controlled material modification (doping/strain) has parallels in controlling coupling strengths or interaction parameters in quantum systems.
